hero.title: The Moon and Mars begin on Earth
hero.lead: Some deserts, volcanoes and polar valleys on Earth closely resemble the places proposed for bases on the Moon and Mars. They're called analogs: crews train there and technology is tested before leaving the planet.
hero.today: Today the Moon is about {{km}} km away, and Mars about {{millions}} million km: its light takes {{minutes}} minutes to reach us.

globe.title: Pick a place and see its twin

hint.mars: Tap a point on the globe or a name in the list to see its twin on Mars.
hint.moon: Tap a point on the globe or a name in the list to see its twin on the Moon.

criteria.title: How we measure similarity
criteria.intro: We compare each place on Earth with every base on the Moon and Mars using the same three measurements. Each one gives a similarity from 0 to 100, and the percentage you see is their average. The values are provisional: the team is still reviewing the formulas.
criteria.temperature: The average gap between day and night temperatures over a year. On Earth it is measured in °C and on the bases in K: a 1 °C difference equals 1 K.
criteria.history: Missions and studies that have already used the place to rehearse exploring another world.
criteria.topography: How much the ground rises and falls: the standard deviation of nine elevations measured on a 3 × 3 grid a few kilometres wide.
criteria.cold: The share of the 12 months whose average temperature is below 0 °C. Every base scores 100, so here it measures how cold the place on Earth is.

locations.title: Twin places on Earth
locations.intro: Each one resembles a proposed base on the Moon or Mars. They are called analogs: because of that resemblance, crews train and technology is tested there. Open any of them to compare it with its twin.
